posts.title: A calmer desk starts with the little things.
posts.excerpt: You don't need a whole new setup. Sometimes, a place for that one cable is enough.
posts.author: Mekanto journal
posts.intro: The cable slips behind the desk. You reach for it, knock a pen onto the floor, and wonder how such a small thing became so irritating. A good desk doesn't have to look like a showroom. It just needs to make the things you do every day a little easier. Before buying another organizer, spend a day noticing what gets in your way. That observation is often the most useful part of the design process.

sections.heading: Start with one recurring annoyance
paragraphs: Pick the thing you fix more than once a day. It might be a charging cable that won't stay put, an adapter that travels between drawers, or a small circuit board sitting on a stack of receipts. Solve that first.

For a cable, the right organizer depends on how you use it. A cable you unplug often needs a channel you can reach with one hand. A cable that stays connected may be better routed behind the desk. The best-looking part isn't useful if it makes your routine harder.

sections.heading: Measure the space you actually have
paragraphs: A product photo won't tell you whether a part fits under your monitor. Measure the available width, depth, and height, and leave space for your hand. For cable clips, measure the cable jacket and check whether the larger connector needs to pass through.
A paper rectangle cut to the proposed footprint is a surprisingly good prototype. Put it on the desk for a day. If it keeps getting in the way, change the dimensions before printing anything.

sections.heading: Let the material do its job
paragraphs: For an indoor organizer away from heat, PLA is a useful material to discuss with your printer. If a part will flex repeatedly or sit near warm electronics, describe that use before choosing a material. Shape, wall thickness, and print orientation matter too.

Visible layer lines are part of an FDM print. We like to treat them as a texture to work with, rather than pretend the object came from an injection mold. Simple shapes and a considered color can make a practical part feel at home.

sections.heading: Make room for the next small improvement
paragraphs: Try one change for a week before adding more. A tidy desk is useful only if it's easy to keep that way. Keep what helps, move what doesn't, and leave yourself some empty space.
If a standard organizer almost works, note what you would change. A few millimeters of extra clearance or a different cable channel may be all a custom version needs.

posts.title: PLA, PETG or ASA? Start with where it will live.
posts.excerpt: A plain-language guide to choosing a material by its job, not just its color.
posts.author: Mekanto journal
posts.intro: It's easy to choose a filament by color. It's more useful to begin with three questions: will the part get warm, will it live outside, and will it need to bend? The answers narrow the field before you get lost in material names. This is a starting point for a conversation about a print, rather than a guarantee that any one plastic will suit your project.

sections.heading: PLA: a starting point for indoor objects
paragraphs: PLA is commonly used for models, prototypes, and everyday indoor objects. It prints readily and can hold fine details well. A desk tray or a non-loaded decorative part is a sensible place to start discussing it.

Heat changes the conversation. Don't assume a part that works on a desk will keep its shape in a hot car or beside a warm device. Share the expected temperature with your printer and check the specific filament manufacturer's data.

sections.heading: PETG: useful for many practical parts
paragraphs: PETG is often chosen for functional prints. Prusa describes it as tough, with good layer adhesion, and useful for mechanical parts. It can be a candidate for electronics enclosures and brackets, depending on the design and operating conditions.

A material name isn't a strength rating for the finished part. Thin sections, fastener loads, and the direction of printed layers can all change how the part behaves. A prototype is still worth testing.

sections.heading: ASA: consider it for outdoor exposure
paragraphs: ASA is a candidate when UV exposure and outdoor use matter. Prusa's material guide highlights its UV and temperature resistance. Printing it also calls for suitable equipment and a controlled printing setup.

An ASA box isn't automatically waterproof. Seams, cable openings, fasteners, and seals need their own design. Describe rain, sunlight, and mounting conditions rather than just asking for an outdoor filament.

sections.heading: Send the conditions, then choose the material
paragraphs: For a custom brief, describe the part's purpose, approximate size, heat exposure, sunlight, expected forces, and any repeated bending. Add photos of where it will sit if you have them.
That gives your printer enough context to discuss material, orientation, and a useful first prototype. The color choice can come after the part has a clear job.

posts.title: Before you print that enclosure, check these five things.
posts.excerpt: Ports, cables, airflow, mounting, and the small clearances that make a big difference.
posts.author: Mekanto journal
posts.intro: An enclosure can look perfect on a screen and still be frustrating on the workbench. The USB plug won't seat. The lid touches a connector. There's nowhere for the wires to go. Most of these problems are easier to catch in a brief than after a full print. If you're planning a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, or sensor enclosure, a few careful measurements give the project a much better starting point.

sections.heading: 1. Identify the exact board
paragraphs: Record the board name and revision, overall dimensions, mounting-hole positions, and the tallest component. Similar-looking development boards can have different port layouts. Use the manufacturer's mechanical drawing when available, and verify it against the board in your hand.

sections.heading: 2. Measure the connectors as well
paragraphs: An opening sized for a USB socket might be too small for the plastic shell around your cable's plug. Try the actual cable and allow room to grip it. Think about the bend immediately outside the enclosure, especially when it will sit against a wall.

sections.heading: 3. Give heat a way out
paragraphs: List the board's cooler, fan, and other heat-producing parts. Leave clearance around those components and plan where air can enter and leave. Test the assembled project under its expected workload; a vent pattern alone doesn't establish thermal performance.

sections.heading: 4. Decide how it will be mounted
paragraphs: Will the box rest on a desk, attach to a rail, or screw to a panel? Include the mounting surface and the space available for tools. Make sure the screws can be reached after the electronics are fitted.

sections.heading: 5. Plan for opening it again
paragraphs: A prototype rarely stays finished for long. Think about access to the memory card, reset button, and lid fasteners. Mark which openings are essential and which can wait for a later version.
For the first print, focus on fit. Check the board, cables, and lid before committing to a larger batch. A clear brief and one useful prototype can save a lot of guesswork.
